entries.title: A Thought Without Collision by Adrian Duncan review – a brilliant interrogation of philosophy and wonder
entries.summary: With a character inspired by Wittgenstein, this exploration of the mysteries of the universe draws on multiple philosophical traditionsFor several years I ran community groups that involved reading books aloud with other adults. Sharing the experience of reading in that way made me notice how, when one or more of us was baffled by a story, this bafflement was rarely experienced without an accompan
entries.content:
For several years I ran community groups that involved reading books aloud with other adults. Sharing the experience of reading in that way made me notice how, when one or more of us was baffled by a story, this bafflement was rarely experienced without an accompanying sense of mild anger. It was so easy to make us, the readers, angry – at the characters; at the author; perhaps even at the nature of this reality on which we’d lost our grip. We were confronted with the fact that our capacity to understand the world was limited. We didn’t like that.

Irish author Adrian Duncan’s fifth novel, A Thought Without Collision, takes risks with this bafflement: it relates and conveys an experience of being mystified by the universe. As it opens, in Ireland in 1923, it is becoming apparent that six-year-old Catherine has exceptional academic gifts, and that her father’s farm is failing. In the next chapter, set in 1951, Dr Josef Alois, a Tyrolean émigré academic in his mid-50s, is living in his self-built house on the east coast of Scotland. He is alone until Catherine reappears, “a handsome woman in her mid-thirties”, and now an Oxford professor. The second chapter ends starkly: Alois “is more unwell than he believes and will perish in one month and eleven days”.

Details of Alois’s biography, and aspects of his two books, are drawn from the life of Ludwig Wittgenstein. The novel references the philosopher’s near-contemporaries, GE Moore, Gottlob Frege and Maurice Merleau-Ponty. Like Alois and Catherine, these men laboured to establish a particular understanding of the world. Some pages of A Thought Without Collision present diagrams or passages of algebraic logic. Throughout, descriptions of small, mysterious places (“pockets” in Catherine’s mind, pits dug in the ground, golf holes, a swallow’s nest) are emblems of the other worlds that surround us, intimated but not available to human knowledge. As Catherine’s intelligence becomes increasingly polymathic, her interest ranges from complex mathematics to animal sentience. She pictures hidden worlds in the sky: a “plane of translucent and unconnected fragments above them all”.

The narrative is related in short, alternating chapters that switch between the two time periods. This creates a sense of flickering movement, like chevrons on a motorway: we see Catherine’s life speed by, an effect intensified by Alois’s impending death. It’s a feat of engineering that the story can cut between these two temporalities and their respective revelations, as it plays with multiple philosophical traditions, while navigating the landscapes of the several distinct historical settings to which the novel takes us.

Beyond these accomplishments, A Thought Without Collision does not feel abstruse or tricksy to read. Its mysteries, like the mysteries of the universe, are not here to infuriate reading groups. When Catherine’s father stakes his farm on American stock market investments, we see how floating abstractions are tethered to material realities.

From his debut, Love Notes from a German Building Site, through The Gorgeous Inertia of the Earth, all Duncan’s novels share a meticulous, patient narrative voice. While some have leaned on a blurry psychological disintegration for their denouement, here the conclusions are more definite: with economic gestures, he offers glimpses of the characters’ new worlds. The novel often reads as a realist Irish rural story: hens underfoot, cold black tea on the table, drizzle. Catherine, so dignified, with a bone-deep sadness contracted via childhood tragedy, could almost be a William Trevor character. But in Duncan’s fiction that tradition converges with a cerebral European mode that is drawn to philosophy, architecture, madness and exile. I can’t think of another writer who draws from the same seams in any comparable way.

The prose is exceptionally, perhaps deceptively, straightforward. When Alois makes dinner, he “sets a dark pot on his range to boil. He then lifts a skillet from the wall and begins to heat it up. He takes butter from his tiny pantry and carves a half-inch cube from it. Then he takes a delph pot from a cupboard and from it lifts two eggs, with which to prepare an omelette.”

This physical attention is intense (there’s more detail here than in a cookbook) but not sustained (it isn’t Knausgård), and so the close descriptions, when they come, seem weighted with something other than themselves. What is the “tiny pantry” here to impart? Is it contextual detail, or a metaphor? We might consider the relation to Wittgensteinian language games; the differing positions played by words as they arise from, and become a part of, actions in the world.

There is also a plainer effect of this superfluity of precision, which is that it feels suggestive – like a photorealistic still life, where the careful replication of detail is an occasion to meditate on something seen through it. In A Thought Without Collision, every half-inch cube of butter makes you wonder.

entries.title: The best recent science fiction, fantasy and horror – review roundup
entries.summary: Massif by Garth Nix; Revolution in the Heart: Stories Inspired By Ursula K Le Guin edited by Jonathan Strahan; An Immaculate Deception by Isabela Livino; Serenity Falls by CJ TudorMassif by Garth Nix (Gollancz, £25)The bestselling fantasy author’s first science fiction novel for adults is set three centuries from now, when humanity has spread out to the stars. The colonisation of other planets has
entries.content:
Massif by Garth Nix (Gollancz, £25)

The bestselling fantasy author’s first science fiction novel for adults is set three centuries from now, when humanity has spread out to the stars. The colonisation of other planets has been enabled by contact with mysterious aliens, and with much of the population split into competing economic spheres, war over territory is raging between the two biggest: United Earth Government and the Mars and Beyond Prosperity Sphere. This war in space is possible only because the godlike aliens continue to supply us with spaceships – but why? What do they want? Answers must await a sequel to this compelling, action-packed space opera with wonderfully weird aliens.

Revolution in the Heart: Stories Inspired By Ursula K Le Guin edited by Jonathan Strahan (Titan, £22)

The authors of these 15 original stories range from the well-established (Karen Joy Fowler, Kelly Link, Molly Gloss) to newer writers (Chana Porter, Ai Jiang, Vandana Singh). A few make direct reference to Le Guin, but most reveal her influence subtly, by shared interests in questioning established ideas and imagining other ways of living, whether among non-human beings, in the future, on other worlds, or in ours. My favourites include Sarah Pinsker’s Travelling, Home, about a young woman in present-day America seeking her place in the world, Ann Leckie’s Five-Eyed Jane, an ironic look at misunderstandings among aliens, and Karen Joy Fowler’s Blaumont, a dark fairytale that’s as disturbing and thought-provoking today as Le Guin’s The Ones Who Walk Away from Omelas. Probably the best original anthology of the year: a must-read.

An Immaculate Deception by Isabela Livino (Gollancz, £22)

In 19th-century Brazil, the deeply religious Madalena knows she’s sinned with her beloved Leandro, but is sure that when she tells him she’s pregnant he will propose. She blurts out the truth before their carriage is wrecked in a storm: waking later in his house, weak and aching, she sees no love in his eyes, and he leaves her to the care of his friend, the strangely attractive Dr Lobo. The two men insist she must stay until she’s fully recovered, but she is determined to get home. Gothic elements glide into full Hammer horror mode as she learns that Dr Lobo belongs to an occult society given to performing dark magic rituals: there are more revelations to come before the end of this wildly entertaining debut.

Serenity Falls by CJ Tudor (Michael Joseph, £18.99)

The latest creepy thriller from the author of The Burning Girls is set in a planned community in Florida, where everyone is comfortable and law-abiding. But when widower Dan and daughter Sadie arrive from England, having inherited a property, they find a dead body in the swimming pool. It turns out there have been a surprisingly large number of accidental deaths during the town’s 50-year history, while the few people who left were never heard from again. That there’s something sinister going on is perhaps a bit too obvious from the start, but the journey to figure out why is entertaining, with a jaw-dropping finale.

Scion by James Islington (Gollancz, £22)

This fast-moving, violent thriller is narrated by Azure, a professional assassin. The world has become so overcrowded that, with increasingly limited resources, legislation has been passed making it legal to kill the rich “lifers” who take advantage of every longevity treatment available. Azure’s skills are always in demand, but his next job is different: he’s been hired to protect a very old lady from being killed. His own life is on the line, especially after her fortress is breached and they’re forced into the dangerous, overcrowded city, where he may find answers to a mystery from his own past. The inconclusive ending makes it clear there are more instalments to come of this gripping blend of neo-noir cyberpunk.

entries.title: Taipei Story by Rebecca F Kuang review – the torture and hilarity of learning Chinese
entries.summary: An American Chinese student studies Mandarin in Taiwan, in this heartfelt journey of self-discovery and family secretsWhat is Taiwan? A former Japanese colony? A centre of the semiconductor industry? A democracy overseen by American imperialism? China’s next military target? An island of Austronesian Indigenous tribes? Is Taipei a cultural emblem of Taiwan, or just another booming global capital o
entries.content:
What is Taiwan? A former Japanese colony? A centre of the semiconductor industry? A democracy overseen by American imperialism? China’s next military target? An island of Austronesian Indigenous tribes? Is Taipei a cultural emblem of Taiwan, or just another booming global capital out of touch with the rest of the country? What stories will Lily Chen, an American Chinese student at Yale and Rebecca F Kuang’s funny and deadpan protagonist in Taipei Story, discover in this melting pot while spending 10 weeks learning Mandarin?

A prolific maverick with rare satirical wit, Kuang has built a career debunking authoritative institutions. Babel (2022) highlights the prejudices of the British empire through a fantastical Oxford translation institute; Yellowface (2023) transplants a heist thriller into the dark heart of American publishing; Katabasis (2025), a journey into the underworld, gives the academic inferno at Cambridge a new lease of death. Centring on a tough Mandarin language school, Taipei Story explores the torture, hilarity and pretension of learning a second language, but here Kuang also offers a heartfelt journey of self-discovery and family wounds.

Lily sets a clear boundary early on: “I wanted to become Chinese here, on my own terms.” Her classmates soon spot that “Lily is very insecure about her Chineseness”. Kuang renders the toxic dynamics and loneliness of foreign students with tact and heart. But what takes the novel beyond the usual campus relationship drama is Kuang’s meticulous, closeup account of Lily’s determination to learn Mandarin. Lily investigates sentence structures, teases out complex clauses, and gradually holds in her head “longer thought patterns in more nuanced logical relation to one another”. She memorises idioms and appreciates the looser Chinese grammar, compared with Latin and Romance languages. Through short, well-paced, diary-like episodes, where Chinese words appear alongside their English counterparts, Kuang recreates the uncanny process of language acquisition, as if the reader is learning Mandarin side by side with Lily, sharing her joy and frustration.

In her Author’s Note, Kuang says the novel is “about getting things wrong … mistranslation, miscommunication, and misunderstanding”. Where Sofia Coppola’s Lost in Translation has Bill Murray sharing his loneliness with Scarlett Johansson, Taipei Story creates an unlikely romantic comedy about falling in and out of love with a language. The novel sparkles with poker-faced humour about language learning. When Lily thinks she’s improving, her teacher retorts: “you have always sounded like an idiot. It is considerable progress that you can now hear it.” After completing the course, her teacher asks if Lily feels like a different person when speaking Chinese. Lily straightforwardly replies: “I feel younger, and more naive.”

Lily is a captivating character; she mocks herself when she feels taken in, as though authenticity derives from the art of counterfeiting. To master Mandarin, she dutifully immerses herself in Taiwanese culture, visiting night markets, eating local food and living in a grotty private apartment rather than university accommodation. In her mission of “trying to blend in”, she discovers the composite layers of Taiwan’s history, sees the ghosts of China, Japan and America everywhere, and finds “no framework for making sense of” anything. Kuang captures this sensory overload throughout, interweaving the complex politics of food, customs, architecture. This leads to Lily’s realisation that “Taiwan had only ever been passed from occupier to occupier – indeed, to Taiwan’s Indigenous peoples, the Han Chinese themselves were occupiers. So who was I to say any occupier was better than the last?”

China remains a mighty spectre in the novel. Following a bereavement in the Mainland, the book takes a poignant turn when Lily uncovers a family secret that unsettles her assumptions about grief, her grandfather and her mother. Kuang handles this shift with curiosity and empathy, tracing Lily’s investigation in heartbreaking dialogues between mother and daughter. Through this rupture, the novel connects the political history of successive authoritarian governments with a personal story of survival and reinvention. Despite the shock at its heart, the novel sustains its tone of pragmatic equanimity, as when Lily realises: “My grief was not that special … Ask around and every first-, second-, even third-generation Asian American had a sob story somewhere in the family tree.” This tough scepticism towards self and identity drives Taipei Story, as it propels Yellowface and Kuang’s other books too.

Towards the end, recognising America’s weakened influence in the Asia-Pacific, Lily ponders: “What if China invaded Taiwan and it wasn’t free any more?” She imagines missiles “flying at any moment”. She also reflects on how languages “map space differently on to time. In English … the future lay before you. In Chinese, the future lay behind.” Taipei Story is a timely, deeply moving novel that helps us weigh a troubled past against a conflicted present.

entries.title: The Eleventh Hour by Salman Rushdie audiobook review – stories with levity and laughter
entries.summary: The author explores themes of legacy, mortality and loneliness in the first work of fiction since his near-fatal attackFive short stories and five readers make up Salman Rushdie’s collection, The Eleventh Hour, his first work of fiction since the near-fatal attack in 2022 where he sustained life-changing injuries. These tales find the author exploring legacy, mortality, loneliness and the ageing p
entries.content:
Five short stories and five readers make up Salman Rushdie’s collection, The Eleventh Hour, his first work of fiction since the near-fatal attack in 2022 where he sustained life-changing injuries. These tales find the author exploring legacy, mortality, loneliness and the ageing process. In these potentially bleak themes, Rushdie finds levity and laughter, as well as profundity.

Late, read by the actor Naveen Andrews, is a ghost story set in King’s College, Cambridge, where an honorary fellow, SM Arthur, wakes up dead in his college room and wonders if he will be trapped there for eternity. He meets a lonely but very much alive Indian student, Rosa, who is stuck at college for the holidays. Sid Sagar reads The Old Man in the Piazza, an allegory about free speech and how “we have become bar room moralists. Does the thumb point upward. Does it turn down? … We are all now gladiators in the Colosseum of the Thumb.”

The best of the stories, In the South, is narrated by Neil Shah who gives characterful voice to two elderly neighbours in Chennai, India, who spend their days bickering with each other on their porches. They are known as Senior and Junior because one is 17 days older than the other. Despite their cantankerousness, the two draw comfort from one another’s presence. When Junior dies on the street after being toppled by a passing Vespa – on the same day that a tsunami hits the south of the country – Senior comes to understand how “death and life [are] just adjacent verandas”.

Available via Vintage Digital, 8hr 12min

Further listening

Kin

Tayari Jones, Oneworld Audio, 13hr, 10min

Angel Pean and Ashley J Hobbs narrate this sweeping tale of two best friends, born a few days apart in Louisiana, who grow up without mothers. As they get older, fate pulls them apart and they pursue different futures.

Land

Maggie O’Farrell, Tinder Press, 16hr 47mins

Not long after the Irish famine, a cartographer’s son must finish a map of Ireland begun by his father away from the prying eyes of the British. This historical novel by the Hamnet author is read by Dane Whyte O’Hara.

entries.title: What Should My Children Do? by Daniel Susskind review – the case for embracing tech in the classroom
entries.summary: A refreshingly optimistic book that asks us to grasp the educational opportunities of AI, rather than shrink from themIn 1979, the government asked Wilfred Cockcroft, a now largely forgotten maths lecturer from the University of Hull, to write a report about a crisis in the teaching of his subject to children. It was wide-ranging and meticulous, and included a chapter on a technological innovation
entries.content:
In 1979, the government asked Wilfred Cockcroft, a now largely forgotten maths lecturer from the University of Hull, to write a report about a crisis in the teaching of his subject to children. It was wide-ranging and meticulous, and included a chapter on a technological innovation that was suddenly becoming available to the average consumer: the calculator.

Many parents and teachers feared that the gadget would undermine a basic skill and a pillar of education – one of the sacred three Rs – producing generations of dumbed-down drones who could reach for a device in their pockets to avoid the hard graft of arithmetic.

But Cockcroft didn’t see it that way. Instead, he proposed embracing rather than fearing the calculator. Students should be taught with and without one – and tested accordingly.

“Cockcroft is unwilling to pretend that the oncoming wave of technological progress can be dodged,” economist Daniel Susskind writes in his urgent new book.

A former Downing Street policy wonk who is now also a researcher at the Institute for Ethics in AI at Oxford University, Susskind casts himself as the Cockroft of the 2020s. In an era of confusion and hand-wringing (if not outright panic) about the implications of AI, he makes the technologist’s case for breathing, learning and grasping the opportunities it presents.

The maths comparison only goes so far, of course; even accounting for the hubris of the AI industry, its achievements have already wrought changes that now make the calculator seem about as consequential as the corkscrew. But while the scale of the disruption is new, the historical context is, to some extent, reassuring.

The book’s title neatly taps into the techno-angst of the modern parent about a future of extreme uncertainty. If traditionally we passed down wisdom with an open-minded but fairly clear sense of how it might apply to a new generation, “today, it feels like that sense of continuity has broken. In truth, we cannot be sure the advice we gave our children last year still works for the next.”

Susskind, a father of young children himself, tries to anticipate a future of artificial general intelligence (AGI) – when AI will outperform us at every economically useful task. (We now have access, via ChatGPT, Claude and the like, to what’s known as artificial narrow intelligence: systems that are good at performing specific tasks.)

In an AGI world – one that it’s easy to imagine is round the corner after reading Susskind’s book –whole careers but also the very meaning of work will change. Susskind urges politicians, parents and teachers to start paddling into that wave now.

He warns against the folly of “future proofing” when the horizon is so foggy. He recalls the David Cameron government’s rush to teach kids how to code, just a few years before it emerged as one of the things that AI does best. Instead, schools should teach children to learn with and without AI, while also doubling down on the basic skills that we should never lose sight of.

He envisages a future of personalised learning, in which AI-trained teachers will deploy the technology as assistant tutors rather than attempting to cater to 30 children as a blob. Graduates entering white-collar industries that stand to be most disrupted should harness AI to free them from the drudgery of, say, reviewing legal documents in a basement and instead hone their craft earlier in AI-simulated trials. Middle-aged careerists should not “retreat to inherited practices” or kid themselves that they occupy “safe” professions; we must remember the underlying problem our professions seek to solve and reimagine how to do so in an AI-assisted age.

Susskind neatly weaves the conceptual and the practical. And while there was apparently no time in this slim work to consider the more immediate ethical implications of AI (its reliance on stolen creative work, its environmental toll) and the questionable personal qualities of so many AI bosses), as a call to action in the face of an unstoppable tide, his book is at once challenging, compelling and refreshingly optimistic.

entries.title: All About My Mother by Rachael Stirling review – a joyous love letter to Diana Rigg
entries.summary: Beautifully written by her daughter, this is a funny and intimate eulogy to the 60s star of The Avengers who went on to specialise in fierce, complicated womenThe late actor Diana Rigg declined to call herself a feminist, noting: “Why would I burn my bra? I need my bra.” Nonetheless, her ideas on womanhood were ahead of their time. In an interview with Michael Parkinson, she observed how marriage
entries.content:
The late actor Diana Rigg declined to call herself a feminist, noting: “Why would I burn my bra? I need my bra.” Nonetheless, her ideas on womanhood were ahead of their time. In an interview with Michael Parkinson, she observed how marriage was “all rather pagan, don’t you think? … A lot of women see it as security. Well, I’m not a woman who yearns for security.”

Taking over from Honor Blackman as the high-kicking Emma Peel in the 1960s spy series The Avengers, Rigg refused to play subordinate sidekick to Patrick Macnee’s Steed, turning her character into a beacon of female empowerment. When Rigg learned that not only was Macnee paid significantly more than she was, but the camera operator was too, she demanded a raise. She got it, but that didn’t stop the press from labelling her as a grasping diva. Fifty years later, she told Newsnight: “Equal pay. That’s what feminism means to me, only that.”

On the stage and screen, Rigg specialised in fierce, complicated women: Medea, Phèdre, Mother Courage, the wimple-clad Olenna Tyrell in Game of Thrones. Yet in life she refused to take herself or her job seriously. Her fear of appearing earnest led her to decline offers of a biography. Now, six years after her death from cancer, her daughter, the actor Rachael Stirling, has taken on the task of documenting Rigg’s life. All About My Mother is a funny, intimate, often joyous and beautifully written eulogy to a woman who didn’t suffer fools yet remained blithely self-mocking and down to earth. Asked what it meant to be made a dame, she replied: “I think it means I’m not supposed to say ‘fuck’ anymore.”

Blending memoir and biography, Stirling builds a portrait based on her own recollections, plus research into Rigg’s performances, writings, recorded interviews and press cuttings collected and stashed in a trunk by her late grandmother Beryl. The book, Stirling says, “is not a detached narrative … This is what I know, what she said, what I’ve learned, what I want to write, what she wrote and what I think she wouldn’t mind my telling you.”

Wild anecdotes of stars behaving badly include the time Rigg was lured to Benny Hill’s house with the promise of a party, only to find she was the sole guest. When he appeared in the garden proffering a drink and a semi-erect penis, Rigg turned away, shouted “LOOK! PARSLEY!” and scarpered. George Lazenby’s claim – false apparently – that Rigg deliberately ate garlic before their love scene in On Her Majesty’s Secret Service led to a scathing war of words between the two actors via a series of open letters.

As a youngster cutting her teeth on the stage, Rigg was a livewire: funny, rebellious, ambitious, given to corpsing from her own onstage pranks. Landing the role of Peel at 27, she found herself with a throng of male fans who wrote in their droves. Rigg put her mother in charge of letters, some of which took Beryl by surprise. She went to the police about a man who regularly sent clippings of his pubic hair in the post. “It turned out he had been bombarding loads of other women with the fruits of his bush,” notes Stirling. “How he managed to maintain his steady, seemingly luxuriant supply we will never know.”

As a mother, Rigg was doting and intense. She would weep dropping Stirling off at boarding school and in the holidays they were inseparable. “I suppose we became what you could call co-dependent, though I didn’t know the word for it then,” Stirling reflects. In a hilariously stomach-churning chapter called “Squeezums”, Stirling describes their ritual of zapping each other’s pimples using tweezers, a piece of loo paper and perfume as antiseptic.

Stirling followed her mother into acting, and Rigg could be fiercely critical of her daughter. On the rare occasions they performed together, Rigg would treat her less like a co-star than a personal assistant, though Stirling nearly always saw the funny side. Her book doesn’t shrink from her mother’s flaws and contradictions, but it remains, above all, a feel-good tale and a love letter. Now, before the first night of a new play, Stirling eats a grain of her mother’s ashes in order that “I am cloaked in her, shielded and shrouded by her. I am her. My mother is my superpower. She always was.”

All About My Mother by Rachael Stirling is published by John Murray (£25). To support the Guardian, order your copy at guardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may apply.

entries.title: ‘She blazed in and opened my eyes to the real world’: Readers remember Gloria Steinem
entries.summary: To generations of women, the feminist campaigner was an inspiration, a fearless challenger of sexism and domestic violence. Guardian readers share memories of her courage, intelligence, and warmthWhat I appreciated most about Gloria was she let me feel normal. I graduated in engineering as one of three women in a class of over 150. In her world, a feminist was a woman that wanted to be judged for
entries.content:
‘She let me feel normal’

What I appreciated most about Gloria was she let me feel normal. I graduated in engineering as one of three women in a class of over 150. In her world, a feminist was a woman that wanted to be judged for her capabilities and not her gender. She was very inspirational and empowering when I first read her books as a young engineer. Teresa, Switzerland

‘A stalwart in my life’

She was a stalwart in my life and my evolution as a feminist and a supporter of the rights of women. I met Gloria Steinem once, at the very beginning of her career and of my own. Fresh out of Wellesley College, I travelled with a friend, another aspiring journalist, to cover the World Festival of Youth and Students, held in Vienna in the summer of 1959. The festival, it was widely acknowledged, was sponsored by the Soviet bloc; it came in the wake of the failed Hungarian revolt against communism and attracted young people from all over the world. From the US, there were two delegations, one called the New York group, the other the Cambridge crowd. Gloria Steinem was the super-glamorous, gorgeous, dynamic “secretary” of the Cambridge crowd. In her low-cut summer frock and what we called, even back then, “fuck-me sandals” she was a knockout, everywhere, directing operations, arranging for Ella Fitzgerald (no less) to give a free concert, feeding journalists stories, prompts, questions. I don’t think her official title was anything more than secretary, but clearly she was the person in charge. I was not surprised when she emerged several years later as a key figure in the burgeoning women’s movement. Her combination of brains and a well-nourished sense of humour brought strength, wit, and intelligence to the movement. And now, when we really need her like again, she is gone – but I pray her memory will continue to strengthen all of us who care about women’s lives and futures. Nancy Harmon Jenkins, 89, journalist, Camden, Maine

‘A lovely, gracious person’

In March of 2014, I was surprised to see Gloria Steinem got on my uptown 6 subway train here in NYC. It was fairly busy on the train but when someone offered her a seat she declined and said she was just going a couple of stops. She was very smiley and casual and even though it was likely most passengers in the car wouldn’t have known who she was, somehow it was clear everyone knew she was someone. This included a young woman who shyly approached her and they spoke for a few minutes and I should say Steinem looked thrilled to bits about this – just seemed like a lovely, gracious person and – like all true New Yorkers – happy to hop on the subway. Niko Wolf, New York City

‘I owe so much to her courage and strength’

Gloria blazed into my consciousness in high school, around 1975. She opened my eyes to the real world; I could define sexism and rail against it. In my 30s, my nickname, Little Miss Independent, surprised me. I was just living my life as I saw fit. She has given me a beautiful one, filled with love, joy, and travel. I owe so much to her courage and strength. I was blessed to come of age with her voice leading the way. I attended a talk held in a local school gym and travelled to the Woman’s March in DC in 2017. Her voice was manna from heaven. Jean, retired educator, New Jersey

‘The catalyst for my lifelong interest in gender studies’

I was attending Wichita State University in 1972 when Gloria Steinem spoke at a forum there. After she spoke she talked with some of us who attended. She was so warm and friendly. She inspired many of us to work to pass the ERA (equal rights amendment) even though it later failed. A year or two after meeting her I moved to Tehran, Iran. She certainly helped me have a different perspective on the living situations of women in Iran as well as the United States. She was very influential in my decision to study what was known then as women’s studies. She was the catalyst for my lifelong interest in gender studies and in particular issues and problems of middle-aged women around the world. Marlene Ammar, 81, Vancouver, Washington

‘My daughter was in awe’

Growing up in regional Queensland, reading Gloria Steinem’s books, it was like opening a portal to a new world that I wanted to be part of. I never met her but had the honour of hearing her speak on her final trip to Australia in May 2016 at Sydney town hall. I took my then 12-year-old daughter. She was in awe of Gloria, seeing all her books and hearing the excitement of the crowd while we waited for the hall to open. We became involved in some incredible conversations with women there – my daughter was incredulous to hear some of the stories such as [women] having to leave their jobs when they got married in the 1960s. We bought some of Gloria’s books and my daughter started to read them on the train home. It was a truly memorable evening. Toni Wren, 63, Sydney, Australia

‘Because of Steinem I became a domestic violence rescuer’

Because of Steinem I became a domestic violence rescuer after I saw how my mom was ignored by the system in the 1960s. I later helped pass the Violence Against Women Act in 1994. Gloria Steinem was a groundbreaking giant. She was smart and articulate like nobody before her, except Betty Friedan – we were so lucky to have these brave women. They woke us up from a long domestic violence nightmare. They did other things for women’s rights, but I appreciate her singular commitment in the DV space. Nobody was talking about it before. Rest in power Gloria, and thank you. Catherine, retired domestic violence worker, Seattle

‘That quick chat was the best’

When I graduated from high school in 1966, women were simply expected to get married, have babies, and work inside the home. I graduated from high school with honours; graduated from the University of Michigan with distinction; graduated from law school with honours; and passed the Michigan Bar Exam the first time I took it. After law school, I worked as a research attorney for two Michigan Circuit Court Judges and then practised with a highly respected, mid-sized law firm until my retirement. I was an early subscriber to Ms Magazine. I never knew Gloria Steinem and I only had the privilege to meet her once. Sometime during the 1990s, she was invited by the Michigan Bar Association to be a keynote speaker. I took a day off from work and drove myself across the state to attend the meeting. At the reception for Ms Steinem, I thanked her “for making my life so difficult”. She smiled and laughed and gave me a quick hug. And that was it. And even though I’ve met many important people, diplomats, and supreme court justices, that quick chat with her to thank her for helping me to fully become myself was the best. Lanie Anderson, 77, retired attorney, Bloomfield Hills, Michigan

‘Gloria was serious about representation’

My mother, Maya Miller, worked with Gloria on poverty and women’s issues. They were on the Ms Foundation board together, which was made up of a dozen or so women from across the country, across races and cultures – Gloria was serious about representation and knew a lot of very smart women. Most meetings happened back east in New York or DC, but in 1972 Nevada cut welfare payments in half. Knowing this affected mainly women and children, Gloria was one of several celebrities to come to Nevada to protest. There was a big march that shut down the Las Vegas strip. Gloria also came to northern Nevada to picket the legal brothels owned and run by men. Gloria supported my mother when Maya ran for US Senate from Nevada at a time when there were no women in the senate. I did meet her a few times, and remember her as kind. Kind eyes, soft spoken, and usually taking a back seat to listen to the other women in the room. And extremely smart with strategy, and witty at confronting chauvinism and stupid men. Kit Miller, 71, Washoe Valley, Nevada
